hops.title: Say it: what a tree saves for spring
hops.text: While the colors climb the strip, say: "The strip pulls the yellow apart from the green!" The yellow hid under the green all along. In fall, a tree's green breaks down, so its yellow shows. Before the leaves fall, the tree takes back some nutrients and stores them in its branches, trunk and roots for new spring leaves.

hops.title: Point at it: sunny leaves and shady leaves on a red maple
hops.text: On a fall walk, with you right beside your child, stop under a maple that is turning red. Look at the leaves out in full sun, then peek into the shady middle of the tree. Sunny leaves often turn bright red, while shaded leaves inside often show little red. Scientists think the red works like a leaf sunscreen.

hops.title: Compare it: a paper towel sipping up a spill
hops.text: Next time water spills on the counter, let your child touch the corner of a dry paper towel to it while you watch the wet patch climb. The coffee filter strip pulls liquid up through its tiny fibers the same way. Colors that dissolve easily ride farther, and colors that grab the paper sooner stop lower.

audio.title: Three easy ways to talk about hidden leaf colors
audio.transcript:
Hi there! While the colors climb your coffee filter strip, here are three easy ways to make this activity click with your child.

First, a sentence to say out loud during the wait: "The strip pulls the yellow apart from the green!" Kids love this, because the yellow was in the spinach all along, hiding under the green. Trees do something similar in fall: the green in their leaves breaks down, so the yellow finally shows. Before its leaves fall, the tree also takes back some nutrients from them and stores them in its branches, trunk and roots, to help grow new leaves next spring.

Second, the next time water spills on the counter, hand your child a dry paper towel. Let them touch one corner to the puddle and watch the wet patch creep upward. Your coffee filter strip sips up liquid through its tiny fibers in just the same way. Colors that dissolve easily ride higher, and colors that grab onto the paper stop lower down.

Third, on your next fall walk, stay right beside your child and stop under a maple that is turning red. Look at the leaves out in full sun, then peek into the shady middle of the tree. Outer leaves soaking up bright sun often turn glowing red, while shaded leaves inside often show much less red. Scientists think red anthocyanins work like a leaf sunscreen in bright sun, protecting the leaf while it unpacks nutrients.

One sentence, one paper towel, and one peek up into a tree. Have fun!
